Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp's Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Rivera, Chief Financial Officer; and David Patel, Chief Operating Officer. Also with us is Sarah Jenkins, Executive Vice President of Midstream Operations.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Emily, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp delivered solid results in Q2, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust midstream segment performance with record transportation volumes and key infrastructure advancements. Our realized prices benefited significantly from our hedging programs, supporting higher realizations for both oil and gas. We posted impressive proved reserves additions, achieving a reserve replacement ratio well above targets through organic growth. Finally, we continued to strengthen our balance sheet by meaningfully reducing debt levels.

I'm particularly pleased with our progress across these areas, which positions us for sustained value creation. We are focused on executing our capital discipline, capturing shale productivity, and delivering free cash flow to shareholders. Now, to provide more color on our midstream performance, Operator, thank you. Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, our EVP of Midstream Operations, to walk us through the performance of our Midstream segment, with a focus on transportation volumes and infrastructure development.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Johnathan, and good morning, everyone. Our Midstream segment delivered another quarter of robust results in Q2, posting segment EBITDA of $425 million, up 18% year-over-year and representing 32% of our consolidated EBITDA. This outperformance was driven primarily by strong transportation volumes amid sustained upstream production growth in key U.S. shale plays, coupled with disciplined infrastructure investments that enhanced our system-wide throughput capacity by 12% since year-end 2023.

Let me start with transportation volumes, which remain the bedrock of our midstream cash flows. In Q2, total system volumes averaged 2.8 million barrels per day equivalent—up 14% year-over-year and 5% sequentially from Q1. Breaking this down by commodity:

Crude oil volumes hit a record 1.75 million barrels per day, a 17% year-over-year increase, fueled by Permian Basin takeaway demand. Our Matterhorn Express pipeline, which we brought online in late 2023 in JV with MPLX and ONEOK, averaged 85% utilization, transporting 750,000 barrels per day of WTI-priced Permian crude to the US Gulf Coast. This was complemented by our legacy Dorado Pipeline system, which saw volumes rise 12% to 550,000 barrels per day, benefiting from tighter Waha hub differentials—now averaging just $0.75 per barrel discount to WTI, down from $2.50 last year—thanks to new takeaway like EPIC Crude's expansions.

Natural gas volumes grew 11% year-over-year to 4.2 billion cubic feet per day, with strong contributions from the Haynesville and Appalachia. Our Cheniere Connector in Louisiana ramped to 1.8 billion cubic feet per day, supporting LNG feedgas to Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi Stage 3 trains, where Henry Hub basis blew out to a $0.15 premium in June amid peak summer cooling demand.

NGL volumes increased 9% to 450,000 barrels per day, driven by fractionation ramps at our Mont Belvieu facility, where Mont Belvieu OPEX propane traded at a $0.45 per gallon premium to NYMEX, reflecting robust petrochemical exports to Asia.

Regionally, Permian volumes accounted for 62% of our crude throughput—up from 55% last year—while Eagle Ford and Bakken added 15% and 8%, respectively. System-wide utilization stood at 88%, with no material constraints, a stark improvement from the 2022 Permian bottlenecks. This volume growth translated to a 22% year-over-year increase in transportation revenues to $620 million, with realized tariffs averaging $1.42 per barrel-mile, up 4% on modest indexation and new contract amendments.

Shifting to infrastructure development, we've executed aggressively on our $2.5 billion 2024 capex plan, with $650 million deployed in Q2 alone, 70% of which targets high-return growth projects yielding 12-15% IRRs at current strip prices. Key highlights:

Completed projects: We achieved mechanical completion on the 50-mile Green Pine Loop expansion in the Permian, adding 150,000 barrels per day of southbound capacity to our Greyhawk system ahead of schedule and under budget at $180 million. This ties directly into our JV with ExxonMobil's Gray Oak Pipeline, alleviating local bottlenecks and securing 10-year take-or-pay contracts at 95% minimum volume commitments.

In-progress initiatives: Construction is 65% complete on the $450 million Apex LNG Express pipeline, a 42-inch, 1.2 billion cubic feet per day line from the Haynesville to the Lake Charles LNG export hub, with FID in Q4 2023 and in-service targeted for Q3 2025. We're incorporating leading-edge tech here, including fiber-optic distributed acoustic sensing for real-time leak detection—reducing false positives by 40% in pilots—and drone-based ILI tools that cut maintenance costs by 25% versus traditional pigging.

Strategic acquisitions and tech upgrades: Post-quarter, we closed the $300 million tuck-in buy of 200 miles of intrastate gas gathering from a private seller in the DJ Basin, accretive immediately at 10x EBITDA multiple. On the sustainability front, we've electrified 40% of our compressor stations with Siemens SGT-800 turbines, slashing Scope 1 methane emissions by 30% year-over-year and positioning us for IRA tax credits. We're also piloting digital twin technology with Bentley Systems across our 5,000-mile crude network, enabling predictive maintenance that has already extended asset life by 15% and boosted EBITDA margins to 62% this quarter.

Looking at trends, U.S. dry gas production is tracking EIA forecasts at 104 billion cubic feet per day, with associated gas from Permian drilling up 8% year-over-year, directly flowing to our pipes. Globally, LNG demand growth—projected at 4 million tonnes per annum in 2024 by Shell—continues to underpin our Gulf Coast assets, while OPEC+ cuts have widened Brent-WTI spreads to $8 per barrel, incentivizing more USGC-bound Permian barrels. That said, we remain vigilant on commodity volatility; our 85% fee-based revenue mix and 7-year average contract life provide durable downside protection.

For the full year, we now guide midstream volumes to 2.85-2.95 million BOE per day, up from prior 2.75-2.90, with capex at $2.4-2.6 billion. We're well-positioned to capture the next leg of shale productivity gains, particularly as Permian rig counts stabilize around 290 per Enverus data.

With that, I'll hand it back to Johnathan.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, for that comprehensive update. Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Rivera to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Michael Rivera: Thank you, Johnathan. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.9 billion, up 22% year-over-year. Operating income was $950 million, and net income was $650 million. We generated $850 million in free cash flow and returned $400 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with total debt at $14.8 billion, net debt at $11.4 billion, and $3.4 billion in cash.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q2 earnings call for Apex Energy Corp. I'll now turn to our realized pricing performance, which came in strong despite ongoing market volatility, largely thanks to our disciplined hedging program. As you know, we focus on high-margin assets in the Permian Basin for oil and the Haynesville Shale for natural gas, where we've been ramping up associated gas production from our DUC conversion initiatives.

Let me start with the headline numbers. Our realized oil price averaged $76.45 per barrel in Q2, up 8% sequentially from $70.82 in Q1 and 12% year-over-year. This compares favorably to the NYMEX WTI benchmark, which averaged $81.25 per barrel over the quarter—a modest $4.80 per barrel discount, or 6%, driven primarily by our Permian WTI differentials averaging -$1.20 per barrel due to robust takeaway capacity from new EPIC Crude and Gray Oak pipeline expansions. In the Eagle Ford, where we have a smaller but high-quality position, differentials tightened to -$0.85 per barrel on stronger regional demand.

On the gas side, realized prices were $2.75 per MCF, a 15% sequential increase from $2.39 in Q1, though flat year-over-year amid softer winter demand. This reflects a $0.15 per MCF premium to Henry Hub's $2.60 per MMBtu average—equivalent to about 1.03 MMBtu per MCF on our rich-gas stream. Haynesville pricing held up well at +$0.25 per MMBtu premium thanks to proximity to Gulf Coast LNG export ramps at facilities like Plaquemines LNG, but we saw some pressure from oversupply in the Permian where associated gas flared less efficiently.

Now, drilling into the impact of our hedging programs, which protected roughly 65% of our Q2 oil production and 55% of gas volumes—these overlays added $2.10 per barrel to our oil realized price and $0.18 per MCF to gas, for a total hedging uplift of approximately $45 million in quarterly EBITDA. Without hedges, our oil realized would have been $74.35 per barrel amid mid-quarter WTI dips below $77 on OPEC+ compliance uncertainty and building U.S. inventories.

Our strategy remains layered and conservative: for oil, we had 45% covered by swaps floored at an average $72.50 per barrel (executed in Q4 '23 at then-sub-$70 futures), 15% in collars with $68 per barrel floors and $85 per barrel caps, and 5% in three-way collars for additional upside convexity—$65 floor, $80 sold call, $95 bought call. This mix captured about 70% of the WTI rally from March lows while shielding against the 12% intra-quarter volatility spike tied to Red Sea disruptions.

For gas, 40% was swapped at $2.60 per MMBtu (NYMEX Henry Hub basis), with 15% in costless collars ($2.40-$3.20 per MMBtu), which proved prescient as spot prices briefly touched $2.90 on LNG feedgas demand. We also layered in 10% fixed-price sales to Gulf Coast marketers at $2.75 per MMBtu, hedging basis risk.

Regionally, this hedging discipline shone in the Permian, where 70% of our oil hedges locked in $73 per barrel floors ahead of Waha hub weakness—our realized Permian oil was $75.20 per barrel versus a -$2.50 per barrel WTI differential benchmark. In Haynesville, gas hedges offset a 5% locational basis compression from Enterprise's Haynesville-to-Midland fractionation constraints, preserving our $2.85 per MCF realized there.

Looking forward, we've proactively hedged 55% of Q3 oil production at $74.20 per barrel swaps and collars, 50% for Q4 at $73.80, and 40% into 2025 at $72.50—positioning us well below consensus WTI strips of $78-80 for H2. Gas hedging stands at 45% for Q3 at $2.70 per MMBtu, ramping to 35% in Q4 amid expected winter shoulder pricing. This leaves meaningful upside—about 45% unhedged oil exposure—to rallies from potential Iranian supply risks or stronger China demand, while capping downside from recessionary pressures or accelerated U.S. rig efficiency gains.

Strategically, our hedging isn't just risk management; it's value creation. We've maintained a hedge book cost basis under 2% of EBITDA annually, far below peers like Devon or EOG who've dialed back post-2022 peaks. This supports our $1.2 billion share repurchase authorization and 12% dividend hike announced today, while funding D&C in our 1.2 PUD locations in the Permian Delaware and Haynesville dry gas window. Compared to unhedged independents hammered by 2023's $60 oil troughs, our program delivered 15% higher free cash flow per debt-adjusted barrel.

Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. This is Michael Rivera, CFO of Apex Energy Corp. I'll now walk you through our proved reserves additions for the year, with a deep dive into our reserve replacement ratio—both total and organic—and the drivers behind our strong performance. As you know, maintaining a robust reserves portfolio is the lifeblood of our long-term value creation in this industry, especially amid volatile WTI pricing hovering around $75-85 per barrel and Brent at $80 this past quarter.

Let me start with the headline numbers. At year-end 2023, our total proved reserves stood at 2.5 billion barrels of oil equivalent—up 12% from 2.23 billion BOE at the end of 2022. We added a robust 312 million BOE of proved reserves through the drillbit and positive revisions, net of 2023 production of 223 million BOE. That translates to a total reserve replacement ratio of 140%—well above our internal target of 120% and in line with top-tier peers like EOG Resources and Pioneer Natural Resources, who posted 130-150% ratios in their recent filings.

Even more impressive is our organic reserve replacement ratio of 115%, excluding any M&A activity. This marks our fifth straight year of organic RRR exceeding 100%, underscoring the quality of our asset base and exploration success. For context, the industry's average organic RRR has hovered around 90-100% over the past decade, per Wood Mackenzie data, hampered by maturing legacy fields and capital discipline post-2014 downturn. Our outperformance here positions us to deliver multi-year free cash flow growth without dilutive acquisitions.

Breaking it down by source, as per SEC rules for proved reserves: Extensions and discoveries accounted for 68% of additions, or 212 million BOE. This was driven by our high-impact drilling in the Permian Basin, where we converted 145 million BOE of proved undeveloped—or PUD—locations into proved developed producing reserves through 450 new horizontal wells. Average lateral lengths stretched to 12,000 feet, with proppant intensity up 15% to 2,500 pounds per foot, thanks to optimized frac designs using our proprietary ceramic proppants sourced from local suppliers like Hi-Crush.

Positive technical revisions added another 78 million BOE, primarily from better-than-expected EURs—or estimated ultimate recoveries—in our Bakken shale program. Here, advanced 4D seismic reprocessing and machine learning reservoir models boosted type curves by 18% in our Parshall field analog, mirroring Chevron's gains in the same play. We saw minimal negative revisions, only 12 million BOE, tied to a few older vertical wells in the Eagle Ford that underperformed amid natural decline curves.

Regionally, the U.S. onshore remains our core engine, contributing 78% of additions. In the Permian Delaware Basin, we replaced 110% of production with 162 million BOE added—fueled by third-party seismic data acquisitions covering 1.2 million acres and our "cube development" strategy, stacking 48-well pads to minimize surface footprint and NRI dilution. This stacks up favorably against Occidental's recent CrownRock deal, but ours is all organic, preserving our 45% full-cycle FCF margins.

The Eagle Ford delivered a 155% organic RRR, with 52 million BOE added via windowed laterals targeting the Lower Eagle Ford lime, where we've unlocked 10% higher IPs through dissolvable diverter tech—similar to what ConocoPhillips has deployed successfully. Internationally, our Gulf of Mexico shelf assets added 28 million BOE through tie-backs to existing infrastructure, like our Lucius field extension, benefiting from deepwater FPSO efficiencies amid rising rig rates. And in Guyana, our 15% working interest in Block Z—modeled after ExxonMobil's Stabroek success—yielded first proved bookings of 15 million BOE from appraisal drilling, with pay sands exceeding 300 feet net in Liza analog reservoirs.

Strategically, these additions reflect our disciplined $2.8 billion capex program, allocated 60% to the Permian for high-return D&C, 25% to infill and extensions, and 15% to exploration. We've leaned into digital initiatives like our ApexAI platform, which integrates real-time LWD data with neural networks to predict frac barriers, reducing dry hole risk by 22% year-over-year. Sustainability ties in too: 35% of new PUDs incorporate electrification and CCUS pilots, aligning with IRA tax credits and positioning us for net-zero scopes 1&2 by 2040.

Looking forward, we see 2024 organic RRR north of 130%, supported by 550 Permian wells online and two Gulf wildcats. This de-risks our 10-year inventory of 4,200 locations at sub-$50 breakevens, even in a $60 WTI downside case. Our finding and development costs clocked in at $11.50 per BOE—20% below the peer median per Rystad Energy—driving NAV growth and supporting our progressive dividend, now yielding 3.2%.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call for Apex Energy Corp. Today, I'd like to dive into our balance sheet strength, specifically our debt levels, net debt position, and leverage ratios. As you know, in this cyclical industry, maintaining a fortress balance sheet is paramount—especially amid Brent crude volatility around $75 per barrel and lingering geopolitical tensions in the Middle East impacting LNG spreads. Our disciplined capital allocation has positioned us exceptionally well, and I'll walk you through the details.

First, on total debt: At quarter-end, our total debt stood at $14.8 billion, down 8% or $1.3 billion year-over-year. This reflects our proactive deleveraging strategy. Breaking it down: short-term debt and the current portion of long-term debt is just $1.2 billion, primarily our $800 million revolving credit facility—fully undrawn, by the way, with $4.5 billion of capacity backed by a syndicate led by JPMorgan and Wells Fargo. Long-term debt makes up the balance at $13.6 billion, comprising $7.5 billion in investment-grade senior unsecured notes (maturities staggered out to 2035, with our most recent $1.5 billion 4.25% notes issued in Q1 at a yield below 4.5%, locking in low rates ahead of Fed cuts), $4.2 billion in term loans from our 2022 syndicated facility (average all-in rate of SOFR + 175 bps, or about 5.8% today), and $1.9 billion in project finance for our Permian Basin Phase III water infrastructure, secured against cash flows from our Delaware Basin assets.

We've optimized the profile significantly: 85% of our debt is fixed-rate, with an average cost of debt at 4.6%, down 40 basis points year-over-year, thanks to opportunistic refinancing. No major maturities until 2026, giving us ample runway. Covenant compliance remains robust—net leverage covenant at 3.0x with 120 bps of headroom under our RCF.

Moving to net debt: After subtracting cash and cash equivalents of $3.4 billion—bolstered by $2.1 billion in Q2 free cash flow from our upstream ops—we're at $11.4 billion in net debt. That's a $1.8 billion reduction sequentially and 14% lower year-over-year. For context, our cash pile includes $1.2 billion in highly liquid Treasuries and $900 million earmarked for near-term Permian rig commitments. Excluding lease liabilities, adjusted net debt is $10.2 billion, aligning with our target range.

Now, leverage ratios, which underscore our peer-leading position. Our headline net debt to trailing twelve-month EBITDA is 1.8x, down from 2.3x at year-end 2023 and well below the 2.5x long-term target we outlined at our February investor day. For reference, that's tighter than Chevron's 1.9x, Occidental's 2.8x post-CrownRock, and ConocoPhillips' 0.9x—positioning us in the upper quartile of E&P peers per S&P Global data. Gross debt to EBITDA sits at 2.4x, and debt to book capitalization is 28%, reflecting our $42 billion enterprise value.

Total debt to equity is 0.42x, supported by $18.5 billion in shareholders' equity, up 5% year-over-year on retained earnings and $500 million in share repurchases under our $3 billion program.

Trends and drivers: This deleveraging is no accident. Upstream free cash flow generation—$6.8 billion TTM—has been the engine, with realizations of $68 WTI equivalent in the Permian (65% of production) and $72 in the Eagle Ford. We've executed $2.2 billion in non-core asset sales year-to-date, including our North Sea UKCS interests to Harbour Energy for $1.1 billion, monetizing mature declines while retaining high-growth Guyana pre-salt blocks via our 25% stake in Stabroek alongside Exxon and Hess. Midstream contributions from our DJ Basin gas gathering JV with Kinder Morgan added $250 million in stable fee-based cash.

Technical initiatives have been key: We've hedged 55% of 2025 oil production at $72 per barrel collars and 45% of Q4 gas at $3.20 NYMEX, shielding EBITDA. Capex discipline—$4.2 billion full-year guidance, 85% upstream—keeps us within cash flow. We're also advancing ESG-linked financing: $500 million green bond for CCUS in the Permian, qualifying under ICMA principles, which lowered our blended cost by 20 bps.

Regional commentary: U.S. onshore leverage is pristine at 1.2x net debt/EBITDA, driven by Permian D&C efficiency (down to $7.5 million per well, 20% below peers via our electric frac fleets). International exposure—15% of debt tied to LNG offtake in Mozambique and Brazil pre-salt—is hedged via take-or-pay contracts mirroring QatarEnergy benchmarks. No Russia or Venezuela exposure, unlike some peers.

Strategic insights: Looking forward, we expect net debt to dip below $10 billion by year-end 2025 through $8-9 billion FCF at $70 Brent, enabling 12% dividend growth to $2.40 per share (yield ~3.5%) and $1.5 billion buybacks. We'll maintain BBB/Baa2 ratings, with S&P affirming our stable outlook last week. Risks? A prolonged sub-$60 WTI could pressure to 2.2x, but our $25 per barrel Permian breakeven and variable dividend framework provide buffers. We're prioritizing returns over growth, targeting 15% ROCE—top decile.

In summary, our debt metrics reflect a best-in-class profile, fueling shareholder value in a WTI-back-half $75 world.

I will now turn the call over to David Patel for an operational update.

David Patel: Thank you, Michael. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 500,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought the Matterhorn Express pipeline and Green Pine Loop expansion online, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth and throughput in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives, including electric frac fleets and digital optimization across our assets.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Laura Simmons with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Laura Simmons: Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the proved reserves additions and reserve replacement ratio?

Johnathan Hale: Good morning, Laura. As Michael detailed, our total reserve replacement ratio hit 140% at year-end 2023, with organic at 115%, driven by strong extensions in the Permian and positive revisions in Bakken. This organic growth from 450 new horizontals and advanced modeling de-risks our long-term inventory without M&A, keeping F&D costs low at $11.50 per BOE. We're guiding over 130% organic for 2024.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brian Thompson with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Brian Thompson: Good morning. What are your expectations for realized prices and hedging going into the back half?

Michael Rivera: Good morning, Brian. Our hedging covers 55% of Q3 oil at $74.20 per barrel and 45% gas at $2.70 per MMBtu, with similar levels into 2025. This locks in solid floors while leaving 45% unhedged for upside, supporting FCF even at lower strips. Q2's $76.45 oil and $2.75 gas, plus $45 million hedge lift, highlight the program's value.

Operator: Our next question comes from Karen Lopez with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Karen Lopez: Could you please provide more color on midstream transportation volumes and infrastructure?

David Patel: Good morning, Karen. Sarah covered the details, but volumes hit 2.8 million BOE per day, up 14% year-over-year, with crude at record 1.75 million barrels per day on Permian strength. Completions like Green Pine and progress on Apex LNG Express boost capacity, and our full-year guide is now 2.85-2.95 million BOE per day. Fee-based contracts provide stability.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to Johnathan Hale for closing remarks.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Operator. In summary, we are pleased with our performance in Q2 2024. We remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering value to our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
